questions.stem: Which of the following drugs is commonly used as a first‑line agent to treat acute peptic ulcer bleeding by reducing gastric acid secretion?
questions.explanation: Omeprazole is a proton‑pump inhibitor that effectively reduces gastric acid secretion and is the first‑line therapy for acute peptic ulcer bleeding. Metoclopramide and ondansetron are antiemetics, and sucralfate is a mucosal protectant but not the first‑line acid‑suppressing agent.

questions.stem: Which of the following drugs is most commonly used as a first‑line agent to treat acute peptic ulcer bleeding by reducing gastric acid secretion?
questions.explanation: Omeprazole, a proton‑pump inhibitor, is the preferred first‑line therapy for acute peptic ulcer bleeding because it provides potent, sustained suppression of gastric acid secretion. Cimetidine, an H2 blocker, is less effective. Pylorid is a prokinetic used for motility disorders, and metoclopramide is also a prokinetic with antiemetic properties.

questions.stem: A 68‑year‑old man with a history of coronary artery disease presents with a 2‑week history of increasing abdominal pain and vomiting. He is found to have a perforated duodenal ulcer. Which of the following drugs is most appropriate to reduce gastric acid secretion and promote ulcer healing in this patient?
questions.explanation: Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) provide the strongest and longest‑lasting inhibition of gastric acid secretion, making them the preferred choice for healing duodenal ulcers. H2‑receptor antagonists also reduce acid but are less potent. Sucralfate protects the ulcer surface but does not reduce acid. Cimetidine is an older H2 blocker and is less effective than newer PPIs.

questions.stem: A 68‑year‑old man with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and recent exacerbation is admitted for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. He is on long‑term oral corticosteroids (prednisone 10 mg daily) and inhaled bronchodilators. Which peri‑operative medication is most appropriate to reduce the risk of postoperative respiratory complications while avoiding significant drug interactions with the patient’s current therapy?
options: A. Intravenous methylprednisolone 125 mg at induction
C. Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg at induction
questions.explanation: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction provides adequate peri‑operative steroid coverage for a patient on chronic oral prednisone, has a short half‑life, and is unlikely to interact with bronchodilators. Methylprednisolone 125 mg IV (A) is a higher dose and may lead to hyperglycaemia; dexamethasone 8 mg (B) is a potent steroid but has a longer duration and can cause adrenal suppression. Continuing the same oral prednisone dose (D) does not provide sufficient peri‑operative coverage and may increase the risk of adrenal crisis. Therefore option C is the best choice.

questions.stem: A 68‑year‑old male with a history of chronic pancreatitis presents with acute abdominal pain and a serum amylase of 1,200 U/L. He is started on a pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT) consisting of pancrelipase. Which of the following statements best explains the mechanism by which PERT improves digestion in chronic pancreatitis?
options: It increases bicarbonate secretion from the duodenum to neutralise gastric acid
It directly stimulates the exocrine pancreas to resume enzyme production
It provides exogenous lipase, protease and amylase that act in the small intestine
It blocks the release of somatostatin, thereby enhancing pancreatic secretion
questions.explanation: Pancrelipase supplies exogenous digestive enzymes (lipase, protease, amylase) that act in the duodenum and jejunum to compensate for the deficient endogenous secretion seen in chronic pancreatitis. The other options describe mechanisms unrelated to PERT: bicarbonate secretion is mediated by the duodenum, not PERT; PERT does not stimulate the pancreas; and somatostatin inhibition is not the primary action of PERT.
questions.source: Pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy in chronic pancreatitis
